supposes that the things which are given him are only his
just due, who takes the good that comes his way as though he
had a right to it, fails to perceive God's overflowing gener-
osity, and misses the best in life, the sentiments of joy and
gratitude and contentment. For such a man is of course never
satisfied, and always thinks that his claim exceeds what is
actually given him. God's goodness implies His freedom; and
as His goodness is inexhaustible, exceeding all the goodness
of man, so also is His freedom unlimited, transcending all
human freedom. Hence if we are to experience God's good-
ness we must be prepared also to acknowledge His freedom,
and to silence all claimfulness. For this reason Jesus in His
parable emphasizes God's freedom so sharply as to arouse at
first a shock of offence in His hearer: "Am I not allowed to do
what I choose with what belongs to me?"
Now of course when we speak in these terms of God's
goodness and freedom many tormenting questions arise. Is
God's goodness in reality experienced by all men? Is it
always only their own fault if they fail to perceive how the
gracious goodness of God is active in their own lives? For
example, did the labourers who were hired first experience
the kindness of their master? There are certainly many sad
and tragic destinies in which it is not easy to trace any
manifestation of God's kindness, and indeed there is much
human distress in face of which heart-searching questions
spring to our minds. Even to those who ask these questions
the words of Jesus contain a message of comfort; but our
parable does not examine such questions directly. It pro-
poses to teach us only one thing, namely, the unity of God's
goodness and freedom. And we should not allow our atten-
tion to be diverted from its main purpose by other questions
which receive an answer elsewhere.
However, if we probe more deeply the teaching implicit in
our parable we perceive that indirectly it also contains some
answer to these vexing problems; namely the answer that, if
we forget God's freedom, we shall never be able to become
